Shoshone Mountains
The Shoshone Mountains, in west central Nevada, make up one of the longest mountain ranges in the state.
The range runs in a general north-south direction in Nye and Lander counties.
Named for the Shoshone Indians, the range receives 15 inches or less of precipitation in an average year.
About 58% of the mountain range is managed by the Bureau of Land Management, with the Forest Service in charge of almost 42% of the area.
A small part of the range is occupied by the Yomba Indian Reservation and private land.
The small community of Ione lies to the west of the range, and the Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park is in the west margin of the range adjacent to Ione Valley just south of the Berlin ghost town.
The old mining camp and ghost town of Golden is at the southern end of the range.
US Highway 50 crosses the extreme north end of the range just south of Mount Airy and 16 miles (26 km) west of Austin.
Nevada Route 722 crosses the range at Railroad Pass just north of Iron Mountain after crossing the Reese River Valley southwest from US 50 near Austin.
Basins or valleys surrounding the range include the Ione Valley and the Smith Creek Valley on the west, the Reese River Valley to the east and the Big Smokey Valley to the south.
Nevada Route 844 crosses the Paradise Range northeast of Gabbs and crosses the Ione Valley to the Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park area.

Surrounding mountain ranges include the Toiyabe Range to the east, the Ravenswood and New Pass ranges to the north, the Desatoya and Paradise ranges to the west and the Cedar Mountains of Mineral County to the southwest.

The Musical Times
The Musical Times was an academic journal of classical music edited and produced in the United Kingdom.
Even during World War II it continued to be published regularly, making it the world's oldest continuously published periodical devoted to western classical music.
In 1947 a two-volume compilation of material from the first 100 years of the magazine, edited by Percy Scholes, was published.
The journal originally appeared monthly but became a quarterly publication in 2004.
Alfred Novello (1844–1853, 1856–1863) championed accessible sacred music and church repertoire, hoping to improve the standard of choral singing in places of worship.
Cowden Clarke wrote a long series of articles called 'Music among the Poets', and induced her literary friend Leigh Hunt to contribute.

William Alexander Barrett (1887–1891, also chief music critic of the Morning Post) and music critic Edgar Frederick Jacques (1892–1897) guided the journal into a more formal era of critical review, while also entrenching it more deeply in the organ world.
Barrett was an organist and composer, while Frederick George Edwards (1897–1909) was a formally trained organist, serving at several major London metropolitan churches.

Edwards used the pseudonym "Dotted Crotchet" to write "educationally suggestive interviews with musical celebrities", as well as a many articles about "cathedrals, churches, and educational institutions".

The mid-century saw a rapid succession of editors more centrally involved in new musical developments, including Martin Cooper (1953–1956), Harold Rutland (1957–1960), Robin Hull (1960) and Andrew Porter (1960–1967).
In 1967, Stanley Sadie (1967–1987) took the helm, transforming the publication into a globally respected journal.

Archduchess Maria Carolina of Austria (born 1740)

Archduchess Maria Carolina of Austria (Maria Carolina Ernestina Antonia Johanna Josefa; 12 January 1740 – 25 January 1741) was the third child and daughter of Empress Maria Theresa, and Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor.
The disappointment was correspondingly great when, on 12 January 1740, a third daughter was born.
After the death of her older sister Maria Elisabeth on 7 June, she became second in the line of succession, preceded only by her older sister Maria Anna.
Five months later, on 20 October, her grandfather Emperor Charles VI died and her mother inherited the Austrian and Bohemian lands, and with this began the War of the Austrian Succession.
On 24 January 1741, the young Archduchess suddenly became gravely ill with violent seizures, dying around noon of the next day.
Two other sisters were named after her: another short-lived one (born and died in 1748) and another (born in 1752), later Queen of Naples and Sicily.

Balmoral, New South Wales
Balmoral is an urban locality in the suburb of Mosman in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia.
The locality is mostly known for its beach, officially divided into Balmoral and Edwards Beaches.
Expensive residential real estate on the surrounding "Balmoral Slopes" benefits from the views and beach proximity.
The naval depot HMAS Penguin is situated at the eastern end of Balmoral Beach.
Balmoral is named after Balmoral Castle, the large estate house in Aberdeenshire, Scotland called Royal Deeside and a favourite summer royal residence.
The Star Amphitheatre, an open-air temple constructed by the Theosophical Society-related group, was built in 1923–1924.

Intended as a platform for lectures by the expected "World Teacher", believed by the Theosophists to be Jiddu Krishnamurti, it was demolished in 1951, and its foundations used for an apartment building that still stands on the site.
The Balmoral Beach Conservation Area is listed on the New South Wales State Heritage Register.
The area includes Edwards Beach as well as Balmoral Beach, plus the promenade, esplanade, rotunda and Bather's Pavilion, which date back to the 1930s.
As the Balmoral area developed, it became the location for many examples of the Federation architectural styles that predominated from 1890 to 1915.
Balmoral is also the location of Noonee, a heritage-listed home designed by Alexander Stewart Jolly.
The house was built 1918-19 and drew on elements of the American hunting lodge.
Services ran to Wynyard, Lane Cove, Athol Wharf and Chatswood, making it one of the busiest lines on the North Sydney system.
Upon departure from The Esplanade Terminus, at the corner of Mandalong Road, trams travelled south-East along The Esplanade.
After passing Botanic Road, the line swung right onto Henry Plunkett Reserve.
The Balmoral Rotunda is the home of Shakespeare by the Sea, a summer outdoor event.
Other notable events include the annual Mudgee Wine Festival and the annual Carols By Candlelight hosted at the Rotunda in December.
The Rotunda and Rocky Point Island are also popular for wedding ceremonies and photographs.
Organisations and facilities include Balmoral Oval, a substantial netted swimming area (Balmoral Baths), Balmoral Sailing Club, a sea scout troop, and two swimming clubs.
The locality has views across the entrance to Middle Harbour to North Head, Manly, and Clontarf.
The harbour beaches face north east and is sheltered from ocean swell by Middle Head.

The conservation area includes the promenade, the esplanade, the Rotunda and the Bathers' Pavilion, which date back to the 1930s.

Bocconi University or Università Bocconi (formally known in Italian as Università Commerciale Luigi Bocconi [universiˈta kommerˈtʃaːle luˈiːdʒi bokˈkoːni] – or simply Bocconi) is a non-profit private university in Milan, Italy.
Its founder, Ferdinando Bocconi, created the university in memory of his son Luigi, who died in the 1896 Battle of Adwa during the First Italo-Ethiopian War.
In 1941, Bocconi moved to its current main campus in Via Sarfatti 25.
Over the decades, the campus has expanded with new facilities, including student residences, research centers, and the business school SDA Bocconi School of Management (established in 1971).
Bocconi is a founding member of CEMS – The Global Alliance in Management Education.
Through its graduate business school, the SDA Bocconi School of Management, the university holds triple accreditation from AACSB, EQUIS, and AMBA.
SDA Bocconi offers MBA, Executive MBA, DBA, executive education, professional development, and certification programs.
Pensionato Building (1956), by Giovanni Muzio, contains dormitories (350 rooms), a canteen, large halls, and faculty offices.
SDA Bocconi Building (2019) houses the new headquarters of the SDA Bocconi School of Management and is located on the site previously occupied by the Centrale del Latte.
Designed by the Tokyo-based SANAA studio, the area also includes the Castiglioni Residence and the sports center.
Leonardo del Vecchio Building (Velodromo) (2001), designed by Ignazio Gardella, is ellipsoid in shape and contains classrooms for up to 150 students each.
Library Building (1962), also by Giovanni Muzio, stands in Piazza Sraffa alongside the campus chapel (San Ferdinando) and other smaller facilities.
Röntgen Building (2007), designed by Grafton Architects, won World Building of the Year at the 2008 World Architecture Festival in Barcelona.
Its designers, Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara, received the 2020 Pritzker Architecture Prize.
Several other administrative and research offices are located near Parco Ravizza and Viale Isonzo.
Residences include Bocconi, Javotte, Dubini, Spadolini, Isonzo, Bligny, and Castiglioni (opened in 2018).
The academic structure includes nine departments: Accounting Computing Sciences Economics Finance Management and Technology Marketing Decision Sciences Social and Political Sciences Legal Studies.
Bocconi's MSc in Finance was among the first six programs worldwide to partner with the CFA Institute and the first in continental Europe.
Its MSc in Management and International Management includes participation in the CEMS Master in International Management, of which Bocconi is a founding member.

MSc programs include Accounting and Financial Management; Artificial Intelligence; Cyber Risk Strategy and Governance; Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence in Health Sciences; Data Science and Business Analytics; Economic and Social Sciences; Economics and Management in Arts, Culture, Media and Entertainment; Economics and Manag...

Programs include: Giurisprudenza Bachelor in Global Law (BGL) Master of Arts in Global Law for Organizations, Business Enterprises and Institutions (GLOBE) Specialized master's include LLM in European Business and Social Law; LLM in Global Tax and Law Governance; and LLM in Law of Technology and Automated Systems.
The school also offers specialized Master programs in areas such as corporate finance, real estate management, food and beverage, fashion, design, and sports management.
In 2011, the European Research Council awarded €5 million to five social sciences and humanities projects led by Bocconi professors.
Past recipients include Fabrizio Saccomanni, Emma Bonino, Vittorio Colao, Nouriel Roubini, Luca de Meo, Francesca Bellettini, and Giuseppe Sala.

Bocconi has been a major recipient of European Research Council (ERC) funding since the program's inception, securing 71 grants across all ERC schemes, particularly in the social sciences and quantitative disciplines, with approximately 35 grants active in 2025.

Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland
The Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland is a charitable trust set up by Andrew Carnegie in 1901 for the benefit of the universities of Scotland, their students and their staff.
The incorporation of the Trust was by royal charter in August 1902, later replaced in July 1978.
The endowment of the Trust on establishment was $10 million (an unprecedented gift, amounting to around 200-times the annual governmental funding of the four Scottish universities at the time).

Under the terms set down by Andrew Carnegie, one half of the Trust's income is reserved for "the improvement and expansion of the Universities of Scotland" with the other half to go towards "the payment of fees of students of Scottish birth or extraction in respect of courses leading to a degree of a S...
In 2004-5, the assets of the Trust amounted to £58million, which enabled awards of £1,667,540 to be made.
The ex–officio Trustees of the Trust are: the Principals of the Universities of Scotland; the First Minister of Scotland and the Lords Provost of Edinburgh and Glasgow.

(Prior to Scottish devolution, the Secretary of State for Scotland held the ex officio post currently occupied by the First Minister.) There are fourteen nominated Trustees, made up of esteemed Scots from various fields.
The Executive Committee, which manages the Trust itself, consists of five of the nominated Trustees and four of the Principals of the Scottish Universities in rotation.
The Trust also enjoys many voluntary repayments by beneficiaries (mainly through legacies) which go towards the Trust's general fund – in 2004-5, these repayments amounted to £134,850.
The Trust intends such scholarships to be the "premier award in Scotland" and they are generally more generous awards than the equivalent from a Research Council.
(For example, in 2008, only 15 out of 142 applicants were successful).
All applicants must be nominated by an academic at a Scottish university and pursue their degrees in Scotland.
The scheme is highly competitive: although the number of scholarships awarded each year is not fixed, it is usually around 12–15, and the number of applicants is usually many times this.
Candidates must be nominated by a university Dean of Faculty, and are for maintenance awards of between two and twelve weeks.
For the five year period from 2013 to 2018, there was an average of 147 applications and 85 scholarships awarded per year, giving an average 58% success rate.
The most successful university in number of awards over the same period was Strathclyde followed by Glasgow.
The yearly income for this fund (£80,000 in 2004-5) goes towards the appointment of two world-class Carnegie Centenary Professors per year for a sabbatical period in Scotland.

Dutch Virgin Islands
The Dutch Virgin Islands is the collective name for the enclaves that the Dutch West India Company had in the Virgin Islands.
The main reason for starting a colony here was that it lay strategically between the Dutch colonies in the south (Netherlands Antilles, Suriname) and New Netherland.
The Dutch West India Company was mainly affected by the competition from Denmark, England and Spain.
Tortola: By 1625, van Dyk was recognised by the Dutch West India Company as the private "Patron" of Tortola, and had moved his operations to Road Town.
In September 1625, in retaliation, the Spanish led a full assault on the island of Tortola, laying waste to its defences and destroying its embryonic settlements.
During the same year, van Dyk lent some limited (non-military) support to the Dutch Admiral Boudewijn Hendricksz, who sacked San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Joost van Dyk himself escaped to the island that would later bear his name, and sheltered there from the Spanish.

Large stone warehouses were built at Freebottom, near Port Purcell (just east of Road Town), with the intention that these warehouses would facilitate exchanges of cargo between North and South America.
Tortola: At this time, the Dutch settlers erected some small earthworks and a three-cannon fort above the warehouse, on the hill where Fort George, Tortola would eventually be built by the English.
Tottola: In 1640, Spain attacked Tortola in an assault led by Captain Lopez.
Two further attacks were made by the Spanish on Tortola in 1646 and 1647 led by Captain Francisco Vincente Duran.
The Spanish anchored a warship in Soper's Hole at West End and landed men ashore.
After a team of scouts returned a safe report, the Spanish landed more men and attacked Fort Purcell overland by foot.
The company changed its policy, and it sought to cede islands such as Tortola and Virgin Gorda to private persons for settlement, and to establish slave pens.
The lack of prosperity of the territory mirrored the lack of commercial success of the Dutch West India Company as a whole.
The island of Tortola was eventually sold to Willem Hunthum at some point in the 1650s, at which time the Dutch West India Company's interest in the territory effectively ended.
In 1665, the Dutch settlers on Tortola were attacked by a British privateer, John Wentworth, who is recorded as having captured 67 slaves which were removed to Bermuda.
Subsequently, in 1666, there were reports that a number of the Dutch settlers were driven out by an influx of British "brigands and pirates", although clearly a number of the Dutch remained.
Britain took the islands from the Dutch as part of the Second Anglo-Dutch War.
During this period, the Dutch occupied the east side of the island, and the British the west.
In 1650, the fortress was abandoned after a conflict with the English.
Tortola: In 1648, the WIC opened a successful post on the island.
In 1665, a small group of Dutch settlers and African slaves were transported to the island to grow cane.
Anegada: Here was a post until 1680, more information is not known.
There are still some ruins to see, and the island of Jost Van Dyke is named after the Dutch pirate.

Emilia (region)
Emilia (Emilian: Emeja / Emégglia / Emélia) is a geographic or historical region of northern Italy.
Its de facto capital is Bologna, with other big cities including Parma, Modena, and Reggio-Emilia.
The name was transferred to the district (which formed the eighth Augustan region of Italy) as early as the time of Martial, in popular usage.
In the 2nd and 3rd centuries Aemilia was frequently named as a district under imperial judges (iuridici), generally in combination with Flaminia or Liguria and Tuscia.
In the 4th century Aemilia and Liguria were joined to form a consular province; after that Aemilia stood alone, Ravenna being sometimes temporarily added to it.

Under the Byzantine Empire Ravenna became the seat of an exarch, and after the Lombards had for two centuries attempted to subdue the Pentapolis (Ravenna, Bologna, Forlì, Faenza, Rimini), Pepin took these cities from the Lombard king Aistulf and gave them, with the March of Ancona, to the papacy in 755, to which, under the name of Rom...

Pope Nicholas III obtained control of Romagna in 1278, but the papal dominion almost fell during the Avignon Papacy, and was only maintained by the efforts of Cardinal Albornoz, who was sent to Italy by Pope Innocent VI in 1353.
Upon the death of Pope Alexander VI it was his successors in the papacy who carried on and profited by what Cesare Borgia had begun.
The Duchy of Ferrara and Comacchio remained under the House of Este until the death of Alfonso II in 1597, when they were claimed by Pope Clement VIII as vacant fiefs.
Modena and Reggio, which were legally Imperial fiefs, but had in fact formed part of the Ferrara duchy, became thenceforth separate dukedoms in personal union under a branch of the house of Este.
Carpi, Correggio, and Mirandola were three of the numerous small fiefdoms which also existed in Emilia and which were generally destined to be gradually absorbed by the two larger states.

The County of Carpy passed to the house of Este in 1530 after the dispossession of the Pio di Savoia family for 'felony' decreed five years earlier by Emperor Charles V, and was elevated to a principality in 1535.

Expressway S3 or express road S3 (in Polish droga ekspresowa S3) is a Polish highway, which runs from Świnoujście on the Baltic Sea through Szczecin, Gorzów Wielkopolski, Zielona Góra and Legnica, to the border with the Czech Republic, where it will connect to the planned D11 motorway.
Its total length is 470.6 km (292.4 mi), but the last 3 km near the border remain closed to traffic until the connecting stretch of the D11 motorway is constructed in Czech Republic.

S3 south of Szczecin overlaps with A6 motorway (see Autostrada A6: History of construction).

Three short sections were constructed in years 2001–2008, also with the first carriageway only.
The new sections had two carriageways, separated by the older stretches (Sulechów–Nowa Sól, Gorzów Wielkopolski bypass and Międzyrzecz bypass) which still remained as single-carriageway.
In 2014–2017/2018, the expressway between Nowa Sól and Legnica (junction with A4) was constructed, and the second carriageway was added on the three older stretches.

The exception was the section Polkowice - Lubin, which was also contracted to be completed in the first half of 2018, but the deal with Salini Impregilo was terminated in 2019 due to extensive delays in construction.
Some of the money allocated for it has been re-purposed to build the S2 expressway in Warsaw.
Later the decision was partially reversed, and in 2014 two tenders were opened for the section between Legnica and Bolków.
The two remaining design-build contracts for the section from Bolków to the Czech border were signed in October 2018.
The section from Kamienna Góra to the border was opened in September 2023, while the section from Bolków to Kamienna Góra was opened in July 2024.

In 1875, the Liberal government of Prime Minister Alexander Mackenzie passed The Supreme and Exchequer Court Act which set up both the Supreme Court of Canada and the Exchequer Court.

The new court consisted of two divisions: the "Federal Court – Trial Division" and the "Federal Court – Appeal Division".

The Trial Division had jurisdiction to hear judicial review of decisions of federal boards and tribunals, including most immigration matters, as well as jurisdiction in admiralty, intellectual property, and disputes involving the federal government.
As time passed, the number of judges was increased and the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court was expanded.

The Appeal Division had jurisdiction to hear appeals of decisions of the Trial Division, as well as to determine applications for judicial review of decisions made by specific boards and tribunals, set out in section 28 of the Federal Court Act.
Decisions of the Appeal Division could be appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, but only if leave (permission) was granted by either court.
The judges and prothonotaries were appointed by the governor in council, namely the governor general of Canada acting on the advice of the federal Cabinet.

The Thai-language printing press at Singapore, previously belonging to London Missionary Society, had been taken over by the American ABCFM.
Bradley brought this ABCFM's Thai printing press from Singapore with him to Bangkok on his arrival.
Dan Beach Bradley, who was more of a physician than a missionary, set up his infirmary, handing out medicines as well as Christian tracts.
Bradley gained popularity and became a sensation among the Siamese elites, who flocked to try the newly introduced Western medicine.
Bradley also discussed with Prince Itsaret (Prince Chuthamani) about the traditional Siamese postpartum practice of laying by the fire.

In October 1835, Chuang Bunnag took the American missionaries John Taylor Jones and his wife Eliza, Stephen Johnson and Dan Beach Bradley, on board his brig Ariel to go on an excursion trip to Chanthaburi.
On his first visit to the Prince-Monk Mongkut in April 1836, Bradley pointed out that Mongkut had been suffering from a stroke, leaving Mongkut with hemifacial paralysis.

Edmund Roberts the American Envoy, who had earlier concluded the American–Siamese Treaty of 1833, brought the treaty that had been ratified by the United States government back to Siam to exchange ratifications, reaching Bangkok in April 1836 with USS Peacock.
Roberts was received by the Portuguese interpreter Luang Surasakhon Piedade in the same manner as his previous visit.
Roberts had another audience with King Rama III on April 16 and the Siamese administrative seals were imprinted on the treaty on April 18.
Edmund Roberts left Bangkok on April 20, going on his mission to conclude treaties with Japan and Vietnam.
When the Peacock arrived in Danang, Roberts was too ill to negotiate anything.
Upon arrival in Bangkok, John Taylor Jones, who had already been vaccinated, inoculated himself with smallpox pus but ended up getting infected with smallpox and fell sick.

In late 1836, Bradley in Bangkok received a batch of smallpox vaccine from the United States and began the first-known vaccination in Thailand by injecting children but the vaccines failed to produce the desired pustule lesions.
Bunti, the long-time leader of the Protestant Chinese converts, left the Baptist Church in late 1836 with discontent.
When Reverend Howard Malcolm, a delegate of the Baptist Board for Foreign Missions, visited the Baptist Mission in Bangkok, only three Chinese Protestants remained in the church.
With Malcolm's presence, John Taylor Jones and William Dean took this opportunity to declare official establishment of Baptist congregation in Bangkok in July 1837.
Upon learning that Bradley had safely inoculated children of American missionaries with smallpox pus, the Siamese king Rama III or King Nangklao initiated the smallpox inoculation campaign in 1838.
In January 1839, Prince Wongsa Dhirajsnid the Royal Physician came to discuss with Bradley.
Smallpox inoculations were carried out extensively among the Bangkokians through 1839 and continued into 1840, the first-known immunization campaign for Thai people, without any fatalities.
Meanwhile, another batch of smallpox vaccine arrived and Bradley took them out to vaccinate people but the vaccines again failed so the Siamese stuck to inoculation.
Bradley then experimented with local smallpox vaccine production from cowpox, composing Treatise on Vaccination in Thai language on how to produce smallpox vaccine for safer immunization.
American missionaries mistook the interest of Siamese elites on Western science as a sign that Siam would become a Christian nation but the Siamese readily filtered out Christianity.
Only a handful of Teochew Chinese people in Bangkok converted to Protestantism.
The missionaries instead became middlemen for the Siamese to learn about Western civilization.
A large number of American missionaries died or left shortly after their arrival and their children usually died young due to hostile tropical climate and prevalent diseases.

Abolition of Siamese royal monopoly for the British and the American merchants by the Burney Treaty of 1826 and the Roberts Treaty of 1833, respectively, caused a great loss of revenue to the Siamese royal court.
William Dean, the Baptist missionary who had been preaching on the Chinese in Bangkok, published First Lessons in the Tie-chiw Dialect in 1841 but left Bangkok for Hong Kong next year in 1842.
In 1843, John Taylor Jones the Baptist missionary, after years of efforts, completed and published the Thai-translated version of New Testament.
Chandler, another Baptist missionary, arrived in Bangkok in 1843 as a mechanic missionary, bringing a new printing press for the Baptist Mission with him.

The 1844 Sino–American Treaty of Wanghia (望廈條約) allowed American access to Chinese treaty ports, resulting in a large number of Chinese-focused American missionaries in Siam moving to China in this period.
Hunter brought steamship Express to Bangkok in 1844 but attempted to sell to the king at an inflated price so the king refused to buy the steamship.
Impactful event came when King Nangklao, out of fear of possible British invasion of Siam, ordered through Hunter a steamship.
Robert Hunter was the influential British merchant in Bangkok who had been the king's favorite.
The Siamese populace, among them the shipbuilders Prince Itsaret and Chuang Bunnag, were astonished by the engine-powered iron-clad vessel, first of its kind ever to arrive in Siam.
Robert Hunter verbally insulted the king for refusing to buy his steamship and threatened to sell it to Vietnam, the archenemy of Siam.
King Nangklao then expelled Robert Hunter from Siam and seized his British Factory.
Caswell wrote The Almanac and Astronomy, which was translated into Thai by Bradley and published in January 1843, which became popular among the Siamese.
Chandler also brought an engine lathe with him, which was purchased by the Prince Itsaret.

In June 1845, the Prince-monk Mongkut, who was then abbot of the prestigious Wat Bowonniwet Temple, invited Jesse Caswell to teach the English language to Mongkut and other monks of the temple in exchange for Caswell being granted a rent-free place adjoining the temple to preach and to distribute books.
Jesse Caswell began his first English class for Mongkut on July 1, 1845, and continued to teach for eighteen months.
The ABCFM then decided in 1846 to dissolve its mission in Siam, prompting Charles Robinson to leave Bangkok but Robinson soon died of illness.
Under Chandler's tutelage, Prince Itsaret completed his first steam engine in 1846.
After four years of efforts, the first native-Siamese-made small steamship, made by Prince Itsaret, was finished in 1848.

On the American Independence Day, the Fourth of July, 1848, Prince Itsaret or Prince Chaofanoi took his steamship to sail in the Chaophraya River for the first time, with the prince himself at the helm steering the ship.
Dan Beach Bradley took his children from Bangkok to Boston in February 1847 to resign from the ABCFM and to find a new sponsor.
Stephen Mattoon and Samuel Reynolds House from the Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions, both Upstate New Yorkers, arrived in Bangkok in March 1847.
Mattoon graduated in theology from Princeton University, while House graduated from the Physicians College of New York, the same medical college as Bradley.
Mattoon studied Thai language and began a new Thai translation of the New Testament, while House carried on Bradley's medical mission.
Before the departures of Caswell's widow Anna and Caswell's son Francis, Mongkut wrote to Francis; "I think of your father mostly as he was my teacher of English.
Meanwhile, Bradley met Sarah Blanchly, a graduate from Oberlin College in Ohio and married Sarah as his second wife in November 1848.
Bradley eventually joined the abolitionist American Missionary Association (AMA) and set sail in October 1849 to return to Siam with Sarah.
The cholera epidemic hit Bangkok in June 1849, killing around 40,000 inhabitants.
Presbyterian missionary Samuel Reynolds House came out to treat patients but contracted the disease himself.
The Siamese king Nangklao ordered a general Buddhist merit-making by releasing domesticated animals to appease the Karma.
After the epidemic, in August 1849, Mattoon and House proclaimed the first Presbyterian Church of Siam, with House elected as the ruling elder.
After premature death of the American envoy Edmund Roberts, Joseph Balestier offered himself in 1838 as the successor to Roberts as Special Agent to oversee American interests in the region.
Balestier left Singapore to return to the United States in 1848, where he pointed out to the Secretary of State John M.
Clayton that no progress had been made to further American interests, in contrast to the rise of British and French influence, in that region.
Balestier urged that the United States should present itself as a powerful nation or else it would fall behind Western peers.
For his efforts, the government, under Zachary Taylor presidency, appointed Joseph Balestier as Special Agent in August 1849 to conclude new treaties with Siam and Vietnam.
Anglo–Siamese relations had been deteriorating since the Robert Hunter Incident of 1844.
In 1848, the Singapore Chamber of Commerce petitioned to the British Foreign Office at London complaining about Siam's new monopoly and the high measurement duties.
Even commercial associations of Liverpool and Manchester urged the British Foreign Office to mend relations with Siam.
Departing from British Hong Kong in February 1850, Joseph Balestier took USS Plymouth under command of Commodore Philip F.
Balestier's bid with the Vietnamese Nguyen dynasty at Danang from February to March 1850 was unsuccessful, however.
Balestier also took William Dean, the Baptist missionary who used to preach in Bangkok, as his interpreter to go on his diplomatic mission.
Brooke was tasked with procuring a new favorable trade treaty from Siam, while also acquiring extraterritorial jurisdiction for British subjects in Siam without provoking any hostile reactions.
As his mission was delayed, Brooke preliminarily sent a letter on HMS Nemesis to inform the Siamese royal court at Bangkok about his imminent arrival.
Joseph Balestier and his retinue on USS Plymouth arrived at the river bar of Chaophraya River on March 24, 1850, where they found the British warship Nemesis already anchoring.
Upon learning about the recent deadly cholera epidemic in Bangkok, Commodore Voorhees refused to go further, even though the American missionaries affirmed Balestier that the cholera had dissapated.

Commodore Voorhees saluted the Siamese elephant flag with 21-gun salute and refused to disembark, leaving only Balestier, William Dean and a Chinese assistant, a total of three people, to ascend to Bangkok.
Unlike the previous Roberts mission of 1833, Balestier had a plethora of American missionaries in Bangkok as his interpreters.
Joseph Balestier met Phraya Siphiphat and other Siamese trade officials in a conference on April 9, 1850, where American missionaries the Baptist John Taylor Jones, his adopted son Samuel J.
Phraya Siphiphat was shocked by the sight of the American envoy Balestier arriving alone with an umbrella held underarm not followed by any honorable retinue but Samuel J.
Siphiphat greeted Balestier with usual Siamese hospitality by asking about Balestier's journey, which Balestier found irrelevant and cut short by demanding an audience with the King of Siam.

Balestier handed a small note from his pocket explaining his mission to Siphiphat and handed over the bare paper of presidential letter to Siphiphat, explaining that this letter came in a sandalwood box with gold lock in proper manner.

Joseph Balestier attempted to reopen the negotiation by sending a letter to the Phrakhlang accusing his younger brother Siphiphat offending him as the representative of the President of the United States.
Dit Bunnag did not reply and Balestier gave up, sending another letter to the Phrakhlang on April 18 requesting a riparian barge to escort him out of Bangkok.

Enraged, Balestier stood up and asked whether or not Siphiphat would accept the presidential letter, to which Siphiphat replied that the presidential letter would be transmitted to the king but the audience would not happen because Balestier's mission was not according to court etiquette.
Joseph Balestier returned to the Plymouth and left Siam on April 24, 1850, without having the presidential letter delivered nor having any audiences with the Siamese king.

Three months after the departure of Joseph Balestier, Sir James Brooke the British envoy, who was the representative of British Foreign Office rather than the East India Company, who had already had a negative view on the Siamese court, arrived at the river bar on 9 August 1850 with HMS Sphinx to join HMS Nemesis already there.
Brooke met Phrakhlang Dit Bunnag the Siamese Foreign Minister at Samut Prakarn and told the Phrakhlang that Siam had earlier concluded the Burney Treaty with East Indi...
Phrakhlang also cited Robert Hunter as the reason why Siam did not want more British people.
As all his proposals were rejected, enraged, Brooke openly declared that Siam had violated the Burney Treaty.
Brooke even offered all Western missionaries in Bangkok a steamer to transport them to Singapore due to the prospect of an Anglo–Siamese War.
Brooke also observed that, despite the king opposing his proposals, he was discreetly supported by the pro-Western princes, presumably the Princes Mongkut and Chuthamani.
Sir James Brooke left Siam empty-handed on 28 September 1850, without obtaining any treaties nor any audiences with the Siamese king.

Brooke wrote to the British Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerston in October 1850 that Siam "may now be taught a lesson which it has long been tempting", also suggesting a gunboat diplomacy to seize Bangkok.
Perhaps the prospect of ascension of a Western-friendly monarch in Siam served to keep the British away from actually attacking Siam.
Mongkut insisted that, however, he would take the throne only if his younger brother the shipbuilder Prince Chutamani or Kromma Khun Itsaret Rangsan also ascended as his co-ruling second king.
Brooke, however, was obliged to return to Britain in May 1851 to face the charges of excessive violence against the natives of Borneo.

After twenty-seven years in Buddhist monkhood, Mongkut ascended the throne as King Rama IV in May 1851 with his younger brother also taking the dignity of co-ruling Second King, becoming the Vice-King Pinklao and taking residence at the Front Palace.
The shipbuilder Chuang Bunnag, son of Dit Bunnag, was appointed Chaophraya Si Suriyawong the Samuha Kalahom or Prime Minister of the South.
Kham Bunnag, other son of Dit Bunnag, younger half-brother of Chuang Bunnag, was appointed Chaophraya Rawiwong as the new Phrakhlang or Sia.

As Mongkut ascended the throne with the support of Bunnag family, he appointed the Bunnags to high ministerial positions; Chaophraya Phrakhlang Dit Bunnag the Siamese Foreign Minister responsible for the Burney Treaty of 1826 and the Roberts Treaty of 1833 was appointed as Somdet Chaophraya Prayurawong the King's Regent kingdom-wide, also called Somdet Chaophraya Ong Yai or the Elder Somdet.
Phraya Siphiphat That Bunnag the younger brother of Dit Bunnag, who had earlier received the American ...

Phraya Siphiphat That Bunnag the younger brother of Dit Bunnag, who had earlier received the American envoy Joseph Balestier in 1850, was appointed as Somdet Chaophraya Phichaiyat the King's Regent in Bangkok, also called Somdet Chaophraya Ong Noi or the Younger Somdet.
Mongkut invited American missionaries and other foreigners to observe his enthronement procession.
During a public audience, Mongkut told the missionaries "Fear not" to pursue what they had been doing.
The new reign marked the change of Siamese attitude towards the West.

Upon his ascension, Mongkut erected a monument over the grave of the American missionary Jesse Caswell, who had earlier taught him the English language and had died in 1848, in remembrance of Caswell as his English teacher.
Earlier in January 1851, however, a fire broke out at the Baptist Mission, during which the printing press and books were destroyed.
Chandler went to the United States in 1851 to urge the American government to make another attempt to conclude a new treaty with Siam.
The Presbyterian Mission in Kudichin, led by Stephen Mattoon and the medical missionary Samuel Reynolds House.
The Congregationalist mission of the American Missionary Association (AMA) led by Dan Beach Bradley.
Mongkut was also more open about new commercial treaties with Western powers in accordance with Western principles.
Lord Palmerston the British Foreign Secretary, upon learning of ascension of a Western-leaning king in Siam, planned to send Sir James Brooke to Siam.
Mongkut had Chuang Bunnag write several letters to Brooke at London, urging Brooke to return to Siam to resume negotiations.

In August 1851, King Mongkut requested the three Protestant Missions to send missionary women to teach English to royal ladies in the woman's quarters of the royal palace, where men were forbidden to enter.
Brooke also found himself unable to return to Siam for his legal charges in London so any British missions to Siam had to be postponed indefinitely as Brooke would never return to Siam.
The Baptist Mission sent Sarah Sleeper Jones, wife of John Taylor Jones.
And the AMA Mission sent Sarah Bradley, wife of Dan Beach Bradley.
Bradley had earlier published Treatise on Midwifery in Thai language in 1842.

In January 1852, King Mongkut assigned American physicians Dan Beach Bradley and Samuel Reynolds House, along with his younger half-brother the Royal Physician Prince Wongsa Dhirajsnid, to take care of a consort and her premature newborn princess, the first daughter of Mongkut, in the inner palace, where men were usually forbidden to enter.
Mongkut's envoys reached Hong Kong in August and was well received by John Bowring the British Consul in Canton and the acting Governor of Hong Kong.
Mongkut then wrote a letter in English to Bowring, inviting Britain to cultivate relations with Siam.
In July 1852, King Mongkut sent envoys to Beijing to ask for formal investiture from the Chinese Emperor per traditional practice.

Gaining the king's favor, Bradley was granted by Mongkut a new place in Bangkok Yai for Bradley's AMA mission and his printing press, prompting Bradley to move from Kudichin, his original place, to his new place in 1852.
Bradley and House were also assigned to tend Queen Sommanat, Mongkut's first queen, who died of postpartum complications in October 1852.
The concept of Manifest Destiny had been pushing the Americans to the frontiers of Oregon Territory, Canton (Guangzhou) and Mexico.
The United States was keen on maintaining its trade with China at a comparable level to Britain.
In the aftermath of the Mexican–American War and Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848, American territories reached the Pacific.
The Americans, however, could not rely on Tokugawa Japan as a friendly local due to Japan's Sakoku or seclusion policy.
In 1842, in response to the Opium War, Japan allowed Western ships to resupply provisions from Japan but any foreigners arriving in Japan would still be imprisoned.
By 1846, there were about seven hundred American whaling ships in the Japanese Seas.
James Biddle led a diplomatic mission with two warships and the presidential letter to Edo Bay (modern Tokyo Bay) in July 1846 but was turned away.
In 1849, David Geisinger sent James Glynn to successfully obtain the release of the Lagoda whalers detained at Nagasaki.
In the aftermath, Geisinger presented a report to the House of Representatives in 1850, portraying the Japanese as cruel and unreasonable.

After these failed missions to establish contact with Japan, also after Joseph Balestier's failed mission to conclude new treaties with Siam and Vietnam in 1850, the United States began to consider political and strategic terms, not only commercial terms, of its policy in the Far East.
San Francisco the "golden gate to trade with the Orient" was the new unique gateway to the Far East, instead of going through Europe and Suez.
Advent of the engine-powered steamships facilitated Trans-Pacific journey even more, bringing East Asia closer to California.

Secretary of State Daniel Webster came up with the idea of a chain of coal supply stations for American steamships from the West Coast to Asia and Japan was considered, in Webster's words, "the last link of the chain of oceanic steam-navigation".
Aulick then proposed to Webster that he would return these Japanese sailors to Japan as a pretext of benevolent gesture to establish relations with Japan.
Perry was appointed as the new commander of the East India Squadron in March 1852 and was also assigned the mission to establish relations with Japan.

President Millard Fillmore wrote a letter to the Emperor of Japan that "The United States of America reach from ocean to ocean, and our Territory of Oregon and State of California lie directly opposite to the dominions of your imperial majesty.
Our steamships can go from California to Japan in eighteen days" and "there is a great abundance of coal and provisions in the Empire of Japan.
Perry departed from Norfolk, Virginia, in November 1852 with the steam frigate USS Mississippi.
Japan, however, was not Perry's only goal as he had been appointed with extensive powers to visit any Asian nations.
By the time that Perry reached Galle in British Ceylon in March 1853, Franklin Pierce had become the new President of the United States.
Simultaneously, King Mongkut had sent some Siamese Buddhist monks on the Siamese square-rigged sailing ship Favorite, earlier built by Chuang Bunnag in 1842, to go on a pilgrimage in Ceylon.
In Galle, Perry met with the captain of Favorite and complimented that the ship Favorite was "one of beautiful form and construction".

Perry wrote a letter to gift a Colt pistol to Pinklao the Second King of Siam, saying that Pinklao's reputation in America for scientific knowledge made him a fitting recipient of the weapon; "The renown which your highness has acquired in America for your attainments in every branch of science induces me to place at your disposal this trifling gift of Mr.
Colt." and "I hope that you will send one of your ships of Siam to America", also thanking Siam for kindness to the late Edmund Roberts du...

Perry continued his journey to fetch another warship USS Susquehanna at Shanghai in May 1853, where Perry met the American merchant in China Townsend Harris, who, like many other Americans, attempted to insert himself into Perry's historic mission to Japan but failed.

Perry departed from Shanghai and reached Uraga Harbor in July 1853 with his two steam frigates USS Mississippi, USS Susquehanna and two sailing sloops-of-war USS Plymouth and USS Saratoga, which were called "Black Shi...
Unlike Biddle in 1846, Perry adopted a threatening stance to impose direct pressure on the shogunate at Edo (modern Tokyo).
The shogunate sent officials to deal with Perry and attempted to divert the ships to Nagasaki but to no avail.
Perry managed to deliver the presidential letter and left Japan for a time being, returning to Hong Kong.
The Second King Pinklao wrote a reply letter to Perry in September.

In October 1853, Perry wrote to the American missionaries in Bangkok, urging them to secure a favorable reception for him upon his anticipated arrival in Siam and assigning them to tell the Siamese government that he promised to assist any Siamese ships going to the United States.
Kalahom Chuang Bunnag replied that Perry should not bring more than two or three warships to Bangkok or else the Siamese populace would panic.
Lord Clarendon appointed Sir John Bowring in January 1854 as the British plenipotentiary to conclude new commercial treaties with the three Asian nations of Japan, Siam and Vietnam.

Perry returned to Japan in February 1854 with even more warships including USS Powhatan, leading to the signing of the Convention of Kanagawa in March, in which the Japanese shogunate government opened Shimoda and Hakodate as treaty ports for American trades, properly assisted the American shipwreckers, not to mis...

Elam Luddington, an American Mormon missionary going to Siam, reached Singapore in March 1854, where he met an English Captain James Trail, who was commanding a barque Sirius trading under venture of the Siamese king Mongkut.

At Singapore, Captain Trail fired gun salutes during a ball of his merchant friend, prompting William Butterworth the British Governor of the Straits Settlements at Singapore to inform Mongkut about Trail's misconduct.
Elam Luddington boarded on Captain Trail's ship Sirius to arrive in Bangkok in April 1854, where Luddington allegedly converted and baptized Captain Trail to Mormonism.
Chandler, who had been in the United States since 1851, returned to Siam with the new Baptist missionary Robert Telford, reaching Paknam Samut Prakarn in June 1854.

Smith came down from Bangkok to retrieve the luggage but the Siamese custom officials at Paknam refused to release any unopened luggage that had not been inspected and Smith did not bring the keys with him, leading to an altercation between Smith and the Siamese officials at Samut Prakarn.
In anticipation of Perry's visit, the Siamese had a chain laid across the Chaophraya River at Paklat (modern Phra Pradaeng) to prevent Perry's warships from going upstre...
In Bangkok, Elam Luddington the Mormon missionary attempted to preach but was rejected by both the Siamese and the Westerners.

In July 1854, an unknown irate Westerner in Bangkok wrote a letter to the British newspaper press The Straits Times at Singapore, informing about the disappointed state of Westerners in Siam towards the new reign.
The letter also recounted the episode of imprisonment of Captain Trail in Siam.
Luddington eventually left Siam in August 1854 on the same ship Sirius with Captain Trail, who vowed to "get even" with the Siamese government for the treatment he had received.
Upon his return from Japan to Hong Kong, in August 1854, having accomplished his mission in Japan, Matthew C.
East India Squadron commander and gave up his promised visit to Siam, citing the depletion of coal supply as his reason.
Smith as the mastermind of this article because Smith was the protagonist of the earlier episode of altercation with the custom officials at Paknam.
Mongkut threatened to expel all the American missionaries from Siam, except for Bradley and House.

Mongkut then had Chaophraya Si Suriyawong Chuang Bunnag gather all the American missionaries at his house to ask the missionaries whether they were the instigators of such article and to ask them to sign a document declaring that the offensive The Straits Times article was untrue, to which the missionaries refused to comply because they found the article to be partially true and signing such doc...
Mongkut also stopped the missionary ladies from further teaching in the Inner Palace.
In December 1854, King Mongkut held a celebration for completion of the newly excavated Phadung Krung Kasem Canal as the outer Bangkok city moat.
When Mongkut went on a tour along this new canal, he saw a Western-style house built closer to the edge of the canal than the regulation allowed.
Relations between Mongkut and the American missionaries, which had been fostered for many decades, were strained to a great extent.
When he found out that this house belonged to Smith, Mongkut became enraged, forbidding all American missionaries from going downstream from Bangkok or they might be shot by Siamese officers.
Mongkut also declared that if any American missionaries found ships to leave Siam he would be glad to let them go.
House, in his memoir, suspected that Captain Trail was the writer of the letter.
Mongkut eventually discovered that it was the Siamese minister Kalahom Chuang Bunnag who had permitted Smith to build the house.

Previously, in July 1854, King Mongkut of Siam wrote a personal letter in the English language to Bowring at Hong Kong, congratulating on Bowring's recent knighthood and appointment as plenipotentiary to Siam.
King Mongkut sent Chaophraya Si Suriyawong Chuang Bunnag down from Bangkok to fetch the British envoys.
Due to the earlier Singaporean newspaper incident, the Siamese government had negative sentiments on the American missionaries.
Chaophraya Rawiwong Kham Bunnag the Phrakhlang or Siamese Foreign Minister forbade any American missionaries to make any contacts with these British envoys.
Mongkut also sent the Isfahan-born Armenian man named Captain Joseph as an English interpreter to greet Bowring.
Harry Parkes objected to Phrakhlang Kham Bunnag, invoking the rights of "unimpeded intercourse", saying that the envoys should be allowed to meet any people in Siam.
Bowring's retinue reached Paknam Samut Prakarn on April 2, where the 21-gun salutes were exchanged between both parties.
Chuang Bunnag did not want the two British warships Rattler and Grecian to ascend to Bangkok for security reasons but Bowring insisted that the warships were parts of his diplomatic retinue.
The three British envoys Sir John Bowring, Harry Parkes and John Charles Bowring were carried by Siamese riparian barges to reach Bangkok on 4 April 1855.
A compromise was reached that only the Rattler was allowed to ascend, while the Grecian was to stay anchored at the river bar all through Bowring's stay in Siam.

The Rattler was also permitted to ascend only up to the Pong Patchamit Fort (in modern Khlong San, Thonburi district), which was about three kilometers downstream from the Bangkok Fort, not allowed to approach the Siamese royal palace.
Bowring demanded that the Rattler should fire a 21-gun salute in Bangkok per Western diplomatic protocol, also as a display of force.
An announcement had to be issued so that the Bangkokians would not panic at the explosive gun salute sounds.
Siamese royal riparian barges carried the envoys to the palace, where Bowring rode on a sedan chair carried on the shoulders of Siamese porters to enter.

After the 21-gun salute by the Rattler in Bangkok, on the same day of April 4, the British envoys were granted a grand audience with the Siamese Mongkut at Amarin Winitchai Throne Hall in the royal palace.
In the Throne Hall, Bowring, Parkes and John Charles sat on three separate chairs in front of Mongkut sitting on a royal throne, while Siamese princes and officials prostrated on the floor.
Bowring presented the gift from Queen Victoria of a golden pendant watch.

Bowring then had a conversation with Mongkut, asking the king who spoke English most proficiently in Siam, to which Mongkut replied that Captain Joseph the Armenian man spoke English best and the American missionaries also spoke good English.

After the audience, on April 8, King Mongkut appointed four Siamese commissioners to conclude a treaty with Bowring; Somdet Chaophraya Prayurawong Dit Bunnag, previously the chief negotiator of Burney (1826) and Roberts (1833) Treaties, also called Somdet Chaophraya Ong Yai or the Elder Somdet Somdet Chaophraya Phichaiyat That Bunnag, younger brother of Dit Bunnag, who had earlier received Joseph Balestier in 1850, also called Somdet Chaophraya Ong Noi or the Younger Somdet Chaophraya Si Suri...
Kalahom Chuang Bunnag expressed his opinion to Bowring that the antiquated Siamese taxation system, which had been reliant on the ethnic Chinese tax farmers, should be reformed.
The American missionaries recounted for Bowring to hear about the previous incidents of the Baptist missionary Samuel J.

Smith going into verbal argument with custom officials at Paknam and the Singaporean newspaper article, resulting in Mongkut restricting their movement, forbidding them to go from Bangkok down to Paknam and beyond, where the missionaries had been going as summer retreat.
The missionaries then beseeched Bowring to intercede with the Siamese king on their behalf.The three Bri...
Extraterritoriality: Britain would appoint Consul to Siam to oversee British subjects in Siam, who would be under British consular jurisdiction instead of traditional Siamese law and judiciary.
Next day, on April 10, the British envoys discussed with Somdet Ong Noi, who seemed to be against their proposals.
Somdet Ong Noi That Bunnag vehemently objected to this proposal, while his nephew Chuang Bunnag supported the proposal.

In the evening of April 10, Chuang Bunnag gave Bowring bad news that the Somdets were likely to reject Bowring's proposals and Chuang himself could not persuade the elders to accede to British demands.
Enraged, Bowring threatened to take the warship Rattler to leave Siam immediately.
Prince Wongsa of the pro-treaty faction called for a conference at his residence the Thonburi Palace.
The two Somdets and Phrakhlang Kham Bunnag called in sick so only two Siamese delegates, Prince Wongsa and Chuang Bunnag, attended.
Bowring also did not attend himself, sending Harry Parkes and John Charles.
Sir John Bowring went to visit Prince Wongsa at the Thonburi Palace, where Bowring noticed Prince Wongsa's American medical diploma displayed at the palace front door.
American missionaries undertook final translation of the treaty, which was presented to King Mongkut on April 16.
Mongkut personally compared the English and Thai versions and made corrections with his own hands.

On April 17, in a private audience, Bowring told Mongkut that the American missionaries had done a great service to Siam as interpreters and translators and asked Mongkut to lift travel restrictions on the missionaries.
Mongkut also told Bowring that he intended the travel restrictions to be temporary.
Next day, on April 18, Prince Wongsa told Bradley that King Mongkut had lifted all travel restrictions on American missionaries, allowing them to go to Paknam.

Six American missionaries, namely Chandler, Bradley, Smith, Mattoon, Telford and Ashmore, jointly wrote a letter to express their gratitude to Sir John Bowring for his role as the arbitrator on their behalf.
The Treaty of Friendship and Commerce between Great Britain and Siam, also called the Bowring Treaty, was signed on that same day of 18 April 1855 at the mansion of the Elder Somdet.
According to Bowring, Chuang Bunnag, whom Bowring called Phra Kalahom, was instrumental to persuading Siam to accept the treaty.
Twenty-one-gun salutes were exchanged between the Siamese Fort and the British warship Rattler.
In legal disputes between a British and a Siamese subject, nationality of the defendant determined jurisdiction.

Cabinet of Uganda
There are 30 Cabinet ministers and 50 Ministers of State in the Cabinet of Uganda (2021 to 2026).
The number of state ministers reduced by one in September 2024 after the death of Sarah Mateke who was the state minister for defence.

If the president does not fire the minister, he/she continues to be a minister, as is the case with Persis Namuganza, who was censured by the 11th Parliament in January 2023 for misconduct but continued to hold office as state minister for housing and even returned after the cabinet reshuffle in March 2024.

According to Section 111 of the 1995 Constitution of Uganda, as amended in 2005, "There shall be a Cabinet which shall consist of the President, the Vice President, the Prime Minister and such number of Ministers as may appear to the President to be reasonably necessary for the efficient running of the State." Ministers are responsible before the Parliament, which can attempt to force their resignation by passing a motion of censure.
